slides.slideTextExcerpt: A market brings buyers and sellers together. Competitive markets contain many participants, so no single buyer or seller sets the price.

slidePreview.alt: Full sample slide introducing markets and competition
slidePreview.title: What makes a market?
slidePreview.subtitle: Buyers and sellers meet, exchange information, and determine what gets traded at what price.

textbookMatches.excerpt: A market is a group of buyers and sellers of a particular good or service. Buyers determine demand, while sellers determine supply.

textbookPagePreview.heading: What Is a Market?
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: The terms supply and demand refer to the behavior of people as they interact with one another in competitive markets. Before examining that behavior, we begin with the setting in which those exchanges take place.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: A market is a group of buyers and sellers of a particular good or service. Buyers determine demand, while sellers determine supply.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: Markets take many forms. Some are highly organized, while in others buyers and sellers are less structured but remain closely connected through price and availability.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Name the two groups that make up a market.

textbookMatches.relationship: Both sources introduce the market as the setting where supply and demand interact. The textbook separates the two roles named together on the slide.

textbookMatches.excerpt: In a perfectly competitive market, the goods offered for sale are alike and the buyers and sellers are so numerous that each has a negligible effect on market price.

textbookPagePreview.heading: What Is Competition?
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: The market for ice cream, like most markets in the economy, is highly competitive. Each buyer knows that there are several sellers from which to choose, and each seller is aware that the product is similar.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: In a perfectly competitive market, the goods offered for sale are alike and the buyers and sellers are so numerous that each has a negligible effect on market price.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: At the market price, buyers can purchase all they want and sellers can sell all they want. For this reason, participants are often described as price takers.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Why can no single participant choose the market price?

textbookMatches.relationship: This passage expands the slide’s definition of competition and explains why an individual participant cannot control price.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: What are the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market?

slides.slideTextExcerpt: The law of demand: when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, other things equal.

slidePreview.alt: Full sample slide showing the demand curve
slidePreview.title: Price up. Quantity demanded down.
slidePreview.subtitle: Holding other influences constant, buyers respond to a higher price by purchasing less.
bullets: Price changes create movement along the curve
Quantity demanded is measured on the horizontal axis

textbookMatches.excerpt: The quantity demanded of any good is the amount of the good that buyers are willing and able to purchase.

textbookPagePreview.heading: The Demand Curve
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: We begin our study of markets by examining the behavior of buyers. To focus the analysis, consider the market for a familiar good and the choices buyers make at different prices.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: The quantity demanded of any good is the amount of the good that buyers are willing and able to purchase.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: Many things determine this amount, but price plays a central role. A table that shows the relationship between price and quantity demanded is called a demand schedule.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Willingness alone is not enough; buyers must also be able to purchase.

textbookMatches.relationship: The textbook supplies the precise definition needed to interpret the quantity axis of the demand curve shown in the lecture.

textbookMatches.excerpt: Because a lower price increases the quantity demanded, the demand curve slopes downward.

textbookPagePreview.heading: From a Schedule to a Curve
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: The demand schedule lists how many units are purchased at each possible price. Graphing these pairs places price on the vertical axis and quantity demanded on the horizontal axis.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: Because a lower price increases the quantity demanded, the demand curve slopes downward.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: The downward slope summarizes the law of demand. Each point on the curve represents one price–quantity pair while all other determinants are held constant.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Trace the curve from a higher price to a lower price.

textbookMatches.relationship: This directly supports the slide’s law of demand and connects the verbal rule to the curve’s downward shape.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: Draw a demand curve for music downloads and show what happens when the price of a music subscription falls.
Explain whether a change in income shifts the demand curve or causes movement along it.
textbookExercises.testedKnowledgePoint: Demand shifts versus movement along the curve

slides.slideTextExcerpt: Income, related goods, tastes, expectations, and the number of buyers can shift the entire demand curve.

slidePreview.alt: Full sample slide showing a demand curve shift
slidePreview.kicker: Not every change is a price change
slidePreview.title: When demand itself changes
slidePreview.subtitle: A change in a non-price determinant moves the entire relationship between price and quantity demanded.

textbookMatches.excerpt: Any change that raises the quantity buyers wish to purchase at every price shifts the demand curve to the right and is called an increase in demand.

textbookPagePreview.heading: Changes in Demand
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: The demand curve is drawn holding many things constant. It need not remain stable over time: an event that changes how much buyers want at a given price shifts the curve.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: Any change that raises the quantity buyers wish to purchase at every price shifts the demand curve to the right and is called an increase in demand.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: A change that reduces the quantity demanded at every price shifts the curve to the left. These shifts are different from movements caused by a change in the good’s own price.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Ask whether the quantity changes at one price or at every price.

textbookMatches.relationship: The passage defines the rightward shift referenced by the slide and distinguishes it from a price-driven movement along the curve.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: List the variables that shift the demand curve and give an example of each.

slides.slideTextExcerpt: Market equilibrium occurs where the supply and demand curves intersect. At this price, quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

slidePreview.alt: Full sample slide showing supply and demand equilibrium
slidePreview.title: Where the market settles
slidePreview.subtitle: Equilibrium is the price and quantity at which buyers’ plans and sellers’ plans agree.
bullets: At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

textbookMatches.excerpt: At the equilibrium price, the quantity of the good that buyers are willing and able to buy exactly balances the quantity sellers are willing and able to sell.

textbookPagePreview.heading: Equilibrium
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: Having analyzed supply and demand separately, we now combine them to see how they determine the price and quantity sold in a market. The two curves are drawn on the same axes.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: At the equilibrium price, the quantity of the good that buyers are willing and able to buy exactly balances the quantity sellers are willing and able to sell.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: The equilibrium price is sometimes called the market-clearing price because, at this price, everyone in the market has been satisfied.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Locate the point where the two curves intersect.

textbookMatches.relationship: This is the textbook’s full explanation of the equality represented by the intersection on the lecture slide.

textbookMatches.excerpt: A surplus puts downward pressure on price, while a shortage puts upward pressure on price.

textbookPagePreview.heading: Surplus and Shortage
textbookPagePreview.contextBefore: Suppose the market price is above equilibrium. Sellers want to supply more than buyers want to purchase, producing an excess supply. Below equilibrium, buyers cannot purchase all they want.
textbookPagePreview.highlightText: A surplus puts downward pressure on price, while a shortage puts upward pressure on price.
textbookPagePreview.contextAfter: The actions of buyers and sellers naturally move markets toward the intersection of the curves. This adjustment is called the law of supply and demand.
textbookPagePreview.marginNote: Use the direction of pressure to predict the next price movement.

textbookMatches.relationship: This adds the adjustment mechanism that explains how a market moves toward the equilibrium introduced on the slide.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: Using a supply-and-demand diagram, identify the equilibrium price and quantity, then show the effect of a price set above equilibrium.

lectureSummary.overview: The lecture introduces how buyers and sellers interact in competitive markets, then builds from individual demand decisions to demand shifts and market equilibrium.
reviewFocus: Distinguish a change in quantity demanded from a shift in demand.
Practice identifying the variables that move the demand curve.
Use shortages and surpluses to explain movement toward equilibrium.
